Polirom is a Romanian publishing house. The company was founded in February 1995 in Iași, a city that remains closely tied to its identity as a publisher. From its earliest days, the house set out to build a catalogue that would reach a broad range of readers.

The first title published by Polirom was For Europe, by Adrian Marino. That book marked the start of a publishing program that has grown steadily over the years. As of 2023, Polirom has published about 8,300 titles, a figure that reflects the scale of its output and the long span of its activity.

The catalogue is organized in a large number of thematic groupings. Polirom has over 60 series and collections, which allow readers to find works by subject, genre, or purpose.

The editorial profile includes both fiction (35%) and nonfiction (65%). This balance means that nonfiction makes up the larger share of the list, while fiction remains a substantial part of what the company offers.

One example of its productivity comes from 2008, when the company published 700 new titles.

Arne Argus was a Swedish newspaper journalist and sports executive. He was born on 21 December 1924 in Bodafors, Sweden, and he died on 8 November 2008.

Argus started his newspaper career as a sports journalist in Nässjö and Eksjö. Journalism was the field in which he first worked, and it formed the starting point for his later involvement in sport at the administrative level.

His work as a sports executive centered on bandy. Argus served as chairman of the Swedish Bandy Association from 1964 through 1970. During the same period, he also took on an international role: he was president of the International Bandy Federation from 1967 to 1971. These two positions placed him in leadership of the sport both within Sweden and at the international level for several years.

Argus also wrote about the sport. In 1998 he wrote the book 100 Bandyfinaler, which is about bandy. The book stands as a written contribution from a man who combined a career in newspapers with leadership in sports organizations.

No. 230 Operational Conversion Unit RAF was a Royal Air Force training unit. It was first created on 15 March 1947 at RAF Lindholme, and it came into being through the re-designation of No. 1653 Heavy Conversion Unit RAF. In this way, the new unit took over from the earlier heavy conversion unit and carried on the work of preparing aircrew for their next aircraft.

The purpose of the unit was conversion training. It converted crews onto the Avro Lancaster, a role that placed it among the units responsible for moving airmen onto larger aircraft. It also converted crews onto the Avro Lincoln, and it converted crews onto the de Havilland Mosquito. The unit therefore handled training on more than one type of aircraft during its existence. The page also records that it trained crews for the Avro Vulcan.

The unit's existence came to an end on 15 August 1952. On that date it was disbanded in order to become the Reserve Training Squadron RAF. Its history, from creation at RAF Lindholme in 1947 to disbandment in 1952, spans just over five years.

Special Hull Treatment is the name given to a method of quieting submarines that was devised in the 1980s. It centers on a simple idea: if a vessel makes less noise, it becomes harder to detect. To pursue that goal, defense contractors coated submarine hulls with a rubberized tile, turning the outer surface of the boat into a tool for managing sound.

The tiles were designed to deaden noise, redirect sound waves, and absorb or contain hull noise. In other words, they were meant to work in several ways at once. Some of their effect came from damping vibration, some from changing the path that sound waves would otherwise take, and some from soaking up or holding in the noise that a hull produces as it moves through the water.

Each tile measured about 12 inches square. A hull covered in such tiles required a great many of them, and each one had to be fitted carefully to the curved steel surface beneath it.

Preparing a submarine for the treatment was demanding work. The hull had to be sandblasted to bare metal and recoated with special paint. Only after that preparation could the tiles be attached. The epoxy used to hold them took about 1 day to harden, so the process could not be rushed and each stage of the installation needed time to set properly.

The first sub to receive this hull treatment was the USS Batfish, c. 1980. Because the approach is dated to the 1980s as a whole, the Batfish stands as an early example of how rubberized tiles were applied to a submarine, combining careful surface preparation, patient curing of the epoxy, and a covering built specifically to control noise from the hull.

Special Hull Treatment was the process, devised in the 1980s, by which defense contractors coated the outsides of the hulls of submarines with a rubberized tile that was designed to deaden noise, redirect sound waves, and absorb or contain hull noise.
The tiles, measuring about 12 inches square resemble an octopus tentacle. They are actually constructed in a quadrahedral formation, in which the bottom sides have an array of holes. The holes connect to a central port in the center of the tile. This port is where a vacuum source is applied to pull a vacuum once the hole tile has been laid on the hull and glued with an epoxy. The epoxy takes about 1 day to harden, after which the vacuum is removed to make sure the tile has a good seal indicated by the vacuum not dissipating.

Anglo-Saxon law was the legal system of Anglo-Saxon England from the 6th century until the Norman Conquest of 1066. It was a form of Germanic law based on two sources: unwritten custom known as folk-right, and written laws enacted by kings with the advice of their witan.

By the later Anglo-Saxon period, a system of courts had developed to administer the law. Enforcement was the responsibility of ealdormen and royal officials such as sheriffs, in addition to self-policing (friborh) by local communities.

The law was not uniform across the whole of England at first. Originally, each Anglo-Saxon kingdom had its own laws. As a result of Viking invasions and settlement, the Danelaw followed Scandinavian laws, so that part of the country operated under a different legal tradition from the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.

In the 10th century, a unified Kingdom of England was created with a single Anglo-Saxon government; however, different regions continued to follow their customary legal systems. Political unity therefore did not bring complete legal uniformity, and regional custom remained an important part of the law until the Norman Conquest of 1066.

The center is the summer home of the Rochester Philharmonic Orchestra. This long-standing association gives the venue a clear role in the season's calendar of live music, with the orchestra making the amphitheater its warm-weather base.

The amphitheater was rebuilt between the 2005 and 2006 seasons at a cost of about $13 million. This was a significant project for the venue, and it changed the character of the space for audiences. Sandvikens Skeppsdocka och Mekaniska Verkstad was a shipyard and mechanical workshop company that operated in Helsinki. Its operating period was 1895–1938, a span of several decades that covered a time of major change for the city and the wider region.

Before and during the First World War, the main customers of the company were the Imperial Russian Navy and the Finnish State Railways. These two clients shaped much of the firm's business during those years, and the company's work was closely tied to their needs.

The Finnish Civil War broke out in 1918, and this event formed part of the historical setting in which the company continued its activities. The company's story therefore spans both the years before the war and the years that followed it.

In 1926 the company sold its shares to Kone- ja Siltarakennus. This sale marked a significant change in ownership and placed the company within the structure of another enterprise. Later, in 1935, Kone- ja Siltarakennus was taken over by Wärtsilä. As a result, the ownership chain linked the Helsinki company to a larger industrial group during the final years of its existence.

The company's operations ended in 1938. Its history is a useful example of how a Helsinki industrial firm could be shaped by its customers, by wartime events, and by later changes in ownership between 1895 and 1938.

Aktiebolaget Sandvikens Skeppsdocka och Mekaniska Verkstad (Finnish: Osakeyhtiö Hietalahden Sulkutelakka ja Konepaja; 'Hietalahti Shipyard and Engineering Works Ltd.') was a Finnish shipbuilding and engineering company that operated in Helsinki in 1895–1938. The company was set up to continue shipbuilding at Hietalahti shipyard, after its predecessor Helsingfors Skeppsdocka, which operated the yard in 1865–1895, had bankrupted.
The company portfolio consisted of the building and repairing of ships and the production of tram and railway wagons, boilers, steam and combustion engines, winches and other products. Before and during the First World War the main customers were the Imperial Russian Navy and the Finnish State Railways. Following the Finnish Declaration of Independence in 1917, the Finnish Civil War broke out in 1918. The yard was closed until the Red Guards had left the city.
Due to recession in shipbuilding the company owners decided to sell the shares to another Helsinki engineering company, Kone- ja Siltarakennus in 1926. In 1935 Kone- ja Siltarakennus was taken over by Wärtsilä, which amalgamated Hietalahti Shipyard and Engineering Works into its own organisation. The yard continued operating under the name Wärtsilä Hietalahti Shipyard after that.

The Old Chestnut Hill Historic District is located in the Newton portion of Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts. It is a residential area recognized for its architectural quality and its carefully shaped setting, and it forms an important part of the neighborhood's identity. Anyone interested in historic homes, landscape character, or the growth of suburban communities will find the district a useful place to learn about how a neighborhood takes shape over time.

The district was first listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1986. This listing recognizes the area as a place of historic significance and places it among the properties across the country that have been formally identified as worthy of recognition. The designation reflects the collective importance of the district as a whole, rather than any single building alone.

At the heart of the district's character are its homes. The district consists of high-quality architect-designed residences on landscaped lots. This combination of thoughtful design and generous, deliberately arranged grounds gives the area a cohesive appearance. Rather than a scattering of unrelated structures, the district presents a unified residential environment in which each house and its surrounding landscape contribute to the overall impression.

The story of the district's growth is closely tied to transportation. Development began significantly after 1886 when the Circuit Railroad brought rail service. The arrival of the railroad made the area more accessible, and this access set the stage for the building of the residences that now define the district. The timing of that development helps explain why the neighborhood is associated with architect-designed houses and planned landscapes.

In terms of scale, the district includes 98-acre and 132 buildings, with 109 contributing. Contributing buildings are those that add to the historic character and significance of the district, and the large share of them here shows how much of the original fabric remains meaningful to its story. The numbers also give a sense of the district's size and of the many individual structures that together make up the historic whole.

Taken together, these features make the Old Chestnut Hill Historic District a notable example of a historic residential neighborhood in Newton. Its National Register listing, its architect-designed homes, its landscaped lots, and its connection to the arrival of rail service all contribute to its lasting importance within Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts.

The Old Chestnut Hill Historic District encompasses the historic residential heart of the Newton portion of Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts.  When first listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1986, the district extended along Hammond Street, between Beacon Street and the MBTA Green Line right-of-way, and along Chestnut Hill Road between Hammond and Essex, including properties along a few adjacent streets.  The district was expanded in 1990 to include more of Chestnut Hill Road and Essex Road, Suffolk Road and the roads between it and Hammond, and a small section south of the Green Line including properties on Hammond Street, Longwood Road, and Middlesex Road.  A further expansion in 1999 added a single property on Suffolk Road.
The district consists of a residential enclave of high-quality architect-designed residences on ample, landscaped lots, that exemplified the development of Newton as a fashionable upper-class suburb.  The area's colonial history begins with settlement in the 17th century by Thomas Hammond and others. Hammond was probably the builder of the c. 1700 Hammond House at 9 Old Orchard Road, considered to be Newton's oldest surviving structure.  The 1723 house at 521 Hammond Street, a substantial Georgian style house, also belonged to the Hammond family.
Development of the area did not begin in a significant way until after 1886, when the Circuit Railroad brought rail service to the area.  A station designed by H. H. Richardson was built at Chestnut Hill in 1883 and landscaped by Frederick Law Olmsted; it was demolished in 1960.  The houses in the district are predominantly Colonial Revival in their styling, although other forms popular into the 1920s are also represented, including Tudor Revival.  There has been only limited new construction in the area since 1942.  The 98-acre (40 ha) district includes 132 buildings, of which 109 contribute to its significance.

The .ki domain is the Internet country code top-level domain for Kiribati. It serves as the national namespace for the island nation online, and it is one of many country code domains used around the world to identify sites connected with a particular country or territory.

The history of .ki involves several organizations. The domain was managed by Connect.com.au from the early 1990s to the early 2000s. During that period, the Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency was the original sponsor of the .ki domain. This arrangement shaped how the domain was first established and operated.

A change came in 2002, when direct management of the .ki domain was transferred to Telecom Services Kiribati Limited. That transfer moved day-to-day responsibility for the domain to an organization based in the country it represents.

Another change followed several years later. As of 2007 the registry of the .ki domain is handled by the Telecommunications Authority of Kiribati. This means the registry function now rests with the national authority responsible for telecommunications.

In terms of technical community participation, .ki is a member of CoCCA.

Despite its long history and its clear national connection, the domain is not widely used in practice. Few sites are using the .ki domain, so it remains a small part of the wider Internet landscape.

Neal R. Brendel (September 12, 1954 – August 25, 2021) was an American rugby union player and lawyer. Brendel played at the inaugural 1987 Rugby World Cup. His test debut for the Eagles was against Australia at the Sydney Cricket Ground on July 9, 1983. He made his last appearance for USA against England at the 1987 World Cup at Concord Oval, Sydney, Australia. Brendel served on the USA Rugby Board of Directors and held various executive posts, commencing in 1996 ultimately serving as Chairman of USA Rugby (2002-2005) and was the first National Team player to ascend to the top leadership post of the Union. In 2017, Brendel was presented with the Craig Sweeney Award (part of the US Rugby Hall of Fame) for his service and contributions to the game and the Union. Brendel was in the first class of inductees into the Virginia Rugby Hall of Fame and was its Honorary Chairman. Brendel also served as a Governor of the US Rugby Foundation.
Brendel began his rugby career at Yale University where he was also an All American NCAA wrestler and in 1976 was awarded Yale’s prestigious William Neely Mallory Award (awarded to the Senior male athlete who “best represents the highest ideals of American Sportsmanship”). In 2009, Brendel helped to establish his law firm’s Dubai office and divided his time between Dubai and Pittsburgh.
Brendel died in 2021 at the age of 66 of mesothelioma.

Yves Brayer (18 November 1907 – 29 May 1990) was a French painter known for his paintings of everyday life.
He was born in Versailles. He studied in Paris at the academies in Montparnasse starting in 1924, and then at the École des Beaux-Arts with Lucien Simon.
Although he was independent and never belonged to a school, he was friends with Francis Gruber, the founder of the Nouveau Réalisme school.
He first exhibited in the salons of 1927, and then traveled to Spain, where the masterpieces in the Prado Museum had a profound influence on him. After a stay in Morocco, he went to Italy, where he won the Grand Prix de Rome in 1930.
He settled back in Paris in 1934, organizing his first solo exhibition. He remained in occupied Paris during World War II.
After the war, he traveled widely to Mexico, Egypt, Iran, Greece, Russia, the United States and Japan, trying to capture the light and colors of each country. He was interested in the techniques of copper plate engraving and lithography and produced illustrations for editions of such authors as Charles Baudelaire and Paul Claudel. He also created murals and wall ornamentations, tapestry cartoons, maquettes, sets, and costumes for the Théâtre Français and the operas of Paris, Amsterdam, Nice, Lyon, Toulouse, Bordeaux, and Avignon.
In 1954 Brayer was awarded to Grand prix des Beaux-Arts de la Ville de Paris, and he was elected to the Académie des Beaux-Arts in 1957. He was president of the Salon d'Automne for five years. In 1977 he was made curator of the Musée Marmottan in Paris, a position he held for 11 years.
Brayer died in Paris in 1990.

Royal Life Saving Western Australia is a water safety, swimming and lifesaving education organisation in Western Australia. It works to teach people the skills and knowledge they need to stay safe in and around water, and it is part of the state's long tradition of lifesaving education.

The organisation was founded in May 1909 as the Royal Life Saving Society of Western Australia. The first meeting was held at the Amateur Sports' Club in Murray Street. In June 1909, rules largely based on those of the Royal Life Saving Society in London were adopted, giving the new body a formal framework for its work.

Over the decades, its reach extended well beyond the city. By the 1970s officers travelled to regional and remote centres such as Paraburdoo, carrying water safety and lifesaving education to communities far from the metropolitan area.

Royal Life Saving WA also recognises courage. It issues bravery awards for lifesaving acts, acknowledging people who have taken action to save others in times of danger.

Kaijudo is an American animated series and trading card game. It serves as a spin-off and relaunch of the Japanese Duel Masters franchise, bringing that earlier property to audiences in a new form.

The animated series was produced by Hasbro Studios. The Kaijudo animated series premiered on the Hub Network on May 5, 2012 and ended on December 28, 2013. The program ran for two seasons before its run came to a close.

The companion trading card game was issued by Wizards of the Coast and first released on June 26, 2012. Wizards of the Coast was also involved with the earlier franchise it grew out of, since the company launched the companion Duel Masters Trading Card Game in the United States in 2004. That earlier card game and the later Kaijudo game therefore shared a publisher, even though they were released years apart.

The franchise was discontinued in 2014, with the TV series cancelled after its second season. Today, Kaijudo is remembered as a combined television and card game effort that relaunched Duel Masters for an American audience, and it remains a distinct chapter in the history of that franchise.

Herbert Southey White (August 1830 – 17 May 1863) was an English clergyman and a cricketer who played in six first-class cricket matches for Cambridge University in 1851 and 1852. He was born at Tivetshall, Norfolk and died at Tunstead, also in Norfolk.
White was educated at Bury St Edmunds Grammar School and at Jesus College, Cambridge, where he was a Rustat Scholar, taking advantage of a fund for the sons of deceased clergy. He played cricket as a middle- or lower-order batsman, though it is not known whether he was right- or left-handed. He top-scored with an unbeaten 28 for Cambridge in the match against Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) preceding the 1851 University Match against Oxford University, but failed to be picked for his Blue. The following season, despite being unsuccessful in other matches, he was picked for the University Match, where he made scores of 5 and 7 in a heavy defeat for his side, which played one man short (10 players against Oxford's 11).
White graduated from Cambridge University with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1853; this converted to a Master of Arts in 1857. He was ordained as a deacon in the Church of England in 1855 and as a priest two years later. He served as curate at Watton, Norfolk and as priest-in-charge of St Matthew's Church, Thorpe, Norwich before settling as vicar of Tunstead and Sco-Ruston in 1858. On 5 May 1863, his wife, Edith Frances, whom he had married in 1858, died at Tunstead vicarage from diphtheria; White died there 12 days later from the same disease.

Oyama taught Kyokushin karate and was sent to New York City in 1966 to provide instruction. That posting marked the start of his long connection with the city. He subsequently ran a dojo in New York for half a century, demonstrating a sustained dedication to teaching across many years.

One of Oyama’s notable achievements was completing the 100-man kumite. A demanding challenge in Kyokushin karate, it remains an important accomplishment in his record as a practitioner.

In 1985, he established World Oyama Karate. Bearing his name, the organization forms part of the legacy he left as a teacher and leader. His instruction in Kyokushin karate, his arrival in New York City in 1966, his many decades running the dojo, his completion of the 100-man kumite, and his establishment of World Oyama Karate together represent the central achievements of his life’s work.

A dozen is a grouping of twelve. The word is used in everyday counting, and the idea behind it is very old. The dozen may be one of the earliest primitive integer groupings, which suggests that people have been gathering things in sets of twelve for a very long time.

Part of the appeal of the number is practical. Twelve is convenient because it has a maximal number of divisors among the numbers up to its double. In other words, within the range from one up to twenty-four, no number can be split evenly in more ways than twelve can. This makes it easy to divide a dozen into equal portions without leaving anything over.

The dozen also serves as the basis for larger units. Twelve dozen are known as a gross. Going one step further, twelve gross are called a great gross. These names give people a simple way to talk about big quantities while still relying on the same base of twelve.

There is also a related term called the great hundred. It is also known as a small gross and is 120 or ten dozen. Although it is built from dozens too, it differs from the gross, since it counts ten dozen rather than twelve dozen. Together, these terms show how the humble dozen grows into a family of useful counting units.

A dozen (commonly abbreviated doz or dz) is a grouping of twelve. The dozen may be one of the earliest primitive integer groupings, perhaps because there are approximately a dozen cycles of the Moon, or months, in a cycle of the Sun, or year. Twelve is convenient because it has a maximal number of divisors among the numbers up to its double, a property only true of 1, 2, 6, 12, 60, 360, and 2520.
The use of twelve as a base number, known as the duodecimal system (also as dozenal), originated in Mesopotamia (see also sexagesimal). Twelve dozen (122 = 144) are known as a gross; and twelve gross (123 = 1,728, the duodecimal 1,000) are called a great gross, a term most often used when shipping or buying items in bulk. A great hundred, also known as a small gross, is 120 or ten dozen.
Dozen may also be used to express a moderately large quantity as in "several dozen" (e.g., dozens of people came to the party).
Varying by country, some products are packaged or sold by the dozen, often foodstuff (a dozen eggs).

Martyrdom in Judaism is an example of Jews doing a kiddush Hashem. The Hebrew phrase kiddush Hashem means sanctification of the Name. In this sense, the act of a martyr is understood as a way of honoring God's Name, and it is closely tied to the idea that a person's conduct can bring holiness into the world.

Public self-sacrifice may lead to being killed for being Jewish. For this reason, martyrdom is often discussed in connection with the experience of Jews who faced death because of their identity and who chose to remain faithful despite the danger. Such an act is seen as a particularly serious form of kiddush Hashem, since it involves giving up one's life in the open.

The opposite idea is chillul Hashem, which means desecration of God's Name. According to Halakha, Jews should avoid chillul Hashem. Taken together, these two concepts form a pair: one describes actions that sanctify the Name, and the other describes actions that profane it and should be avoided.

A martyr in Hebrew is known as a kaddosh. The plural form is often used when speaking of many people who died as martyrs. In modern memory, the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust are known as the Kedoshim. This use of the term links their memory to the long-standing vocabulary of martyrdom and sanctification within Judaism.

The Isle of Pines is a commune in the South Province of New Caledonia. It is a place with a distinctive identity, and it is known to many people by a poetic nickname: l'île la plus proche du paradis. That phrase, which can be understood as "the island closest to paradise," captures the way the commune is often described and remembered.

The settlement of Vao is the administrative centre of the commune of the Isle of Pines. It is the place where local administration is based, and it serves as the focal point of the commune's public life.

The Isle of Pines is also remarkably far from the French capital. It lies 16,830 km from Paris, a distance that underlines just how remote this part of New Caledonia is from the European centre of French government and culture.

Despite that distance, the island has a historical link with Paris. After the Paris Commune in 1871, about 2,800 insurgents were deported to the Isle of Pines. This chapter connects the commune to a major episode in French political history, and it remains an important part of the story of the island.

The natural setting also gives the commune its character. The Isle of Pines has ancient pine tree groves, which are closely tied to the name of the island and form part of its landscape. These groves help explain why the island is so memorable to those who learn about it.

The area has also appeared in popular media. In 2005, Les Aventuriers de Koh-Lanta was set on islands off the Isle of Pines. The program brought the surrounding islands to the attention of a wider audience, adding a modern chapter to the island's public image.

Taken together, these details show a commune with several sides: an administrative centre at Vao, a place within the South Province of New Caledonia, a great distance from Paris, a historical connection to the aftermath of the Paris Commune, a landscape of ancient pine tree groves, and a reputation expressed in its famous nickname. Each of these elements contributes to the picture of the Isle of Pines as a distinctive and widely recognised corner of New Caledonia.

Sir Marmaduke Lloyd (1585–c. 1651) was a Welsh lawyer and landowner, as well as a supporter of King Charles I of England during the English Civil War.
Lloyd was the son of Thomas Lloyd, a precentor at St David's Cathedral, and the nephew of Marmaduke Middleton, who was Bishop of St David's from.  Having studied at Oriel College, Oxford, and Middle Temple, he qualified as a barrister in 1608.  He married Mary Stedman, and the family eventually settled at Maesyfelin, near Lampeter.
Lloyd held the position of King's Attorney for the Marches from 1614, in which year he was also appointed to the Council of Wales and the Marches.  Knighted in 1622, he became puisne justice of Chester in the same year, and chief justice of the Brecknock circuit in 1636.  Official records suggest that he made frequent visits to Shrewsbury. In 1645 he was taken prisoner at Hereford by Parliamentary forces, and remained in custody until 1647.  At the Battle of St Fagans in 1648, he was again taken prisoner.  The date of his will suggests that he died in 1651.
The poet Henry Vaughan at one time served as secretary to Sir Marmaduke.
The eldest of Sir Marmaduke's three sons, Sir Francis Lloyd, also a Royalist, was a Member of Parliament before the war and regained a position of favour following the Restoration of King Charles II of England.

The Ariel was designed by naval architect Carl Alberg in 1961 for Pearson Yachts of Bristol, Rhode Island. The Ariel offered Pearson's early 1960s customers a midsized boat to fill the product line between the very successful Pearson Triton and the smaller Pearson Ensign/Electra. The Ariel shares many of the amenities of the larger Triton including standing headroom (5'10"), berths for four, sink, ice box, freshwater tank and an enclosed head. Other factory options included spinnaker gear and the choice of auxiliary power (Universal Atomic 4 inboard or an outboard in a well).
The Ariel and a later daysailing version, the Commander share a common hull and rig (the Commander has a smaller, more spartan cabin to allow for a very spacious cockpit). Of the more than 50 boat designs Carl Alberg produced after leaving the John G. Alden firm to design on his own, Alberg chose the Commander as his personal boat (Hull #302). This boat was named "ALMA" in honor of his wife and for many of his later years was sailed out of Marblehead, Ma.
Although the Ariel was produced from 1962 to 1967 (for a total of 440 boats), the majority remain in service today.  While many Ariels and Commanders are used for casual daysailing, an active one design racing community still operates in San Francisco. Mickey's Dining Car is a classic diner in downtown Saint Paul, Minnesota, United States. Often searched for under the name Mickey's Diner, it is a well-known landmark of the city's downtown. The building was designed to resemble a railroad dining car, and its appearance reflects that inspiration.

The diner was constructed in 1937 by the Jerry O'Mahony Diner Company of Elizabeth, New Jersey. It opened in 1939, two years after its construction. In 1983, it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, a recognition of its place in the nation's historic record.

From 1939 until the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, Mickey's Dining Car ran in continuous operation at the same location on West 7th Street. That long stretch of service made it a steady presence in downtown Saint Paul for many decades.

After the closure that came with the pandemic, the diner returned to service. It reopened on the morning of October 3, 2024, welcoming visitors once again to its place on West 7th Street.

Carlo Bonavia (died 1788) was an Italian painter known for idyllic landscape paintings, engravings and drawings.  He was active from 1740 until his death.  He is thought to be from Rome, but worked in Naples from about 1751 to 1788.  He was trained in the Neapolitan landscape tradition of Salvator Rosa (1615–1673) and Leonardo Coccorante (1680–1750), but was much more strongly influenced by the work of Claude Joseph Vernet, who visited Naples in 1737 and 1746.
Bonavia's paintings share with Vernet's a rococo palette of pale blues, creamy yellows, pinks and soft green, as well as an atmospheric, rather than analytical, approach to landscape. Like Vernet, Bonavia painted capricci in which real features of the Neapolitan countryside were placed in imaginary settings.  Bonavia's idyllic landscapes were popular souvenirs of the Grand Tour.  Among his patrons were Lord Brudenell and Count Karl Joseph Firmian, the Austrian ambassador to Naples 1753–8. Bonavia had a very successful career and was praised by Pietro Zani in his Enciclopedia Metodica Critico Ragionata delle Belle Arte (1794) as a fine painter of views and history subjects.
The Accademia di San Luca (Rome), the Dulwich Picture Gallery, the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, the Honolulu Museum of Art, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museo di Capodimonte (Naples) and Stourhead (Wiltshire, England), Basildon Park (National Trust, Berkshire, England) are among the public collections having paintings by Carlo Bonavia.

The market mechanism is a way of organizing economic activity in which money exchanged by buyers and sellers is used to optimize distribution. Rather than relying on a central authority to decide who receives what, the system lets countless individual transactions determine how goods and services are allocated. Each purchase and each sale adds to a larger pattern that shapes what is available and who gets it.

A central feature of this system is the role of prices. Prices convey information about what producers should produce. When buyers are willing to pay more for something, the higher price signals to producers that there is a reason to make more of it. When buyers lose interest, a falling price signals that resources may be better used elsewhere. In this way, prices act as a form of communication between people who may never meet, guiding decisions without any single person directing the whole process.

Despite these strengths, the market mechanism is often discussed alongside the question of how far governments should take part in economic life. Government interference can lead to economic inefficiency, because it may distort the signals that prices provide and so push resources away from their most valued uses. This concern is one reason many economists urge caution when considering intervention in markets.

Yet the picture is not one-sided. Modern highways required government planning and allocation, which shows that some projects have depended on public coordination rather than on exchange between buyers and sellers alone. Examples like this are frequently raised in debates about where markets work well and where collective planning has been necessary.

Governments also take part in the economy through broader policy tools. Fiscal policy and monetary policy influence demand through price adjustments. By changing conditions that affect prices, policymakers can affect how much buyers wish to purchase, which in turn feeds back into the decisions that producers make.

Ideas about how to manage money within this framework have also been influential. The Friedman rule was proposed by Milton Friedman, and it remains a notable part of discussions about monetary policy and its relationship to market outcomes.

Taken together, these points show that the market mechanism is both powerful and debated. It relies on money, prices, and voluntary exchange to organize distribution, while questions about government involvement continue to shape how it is understood and applied.

In economics, the market mechanism is a mechanism by which the use of money exchanged by buyers and sellers with an open and understood system of value and time trade-offs in a market tends to optimize distribution of goods and services in at least some ways. The mechanism can exist in free markets or in captive or controlling markets seek to use supply and demand, or some other form of charging for scarcity, to choose among production possibilities. In a free market economy, all the resources are allocated by the private sector (individuals, households, and groups of individuals); in a planned economy, all the resources are owned by the public sector (local and central government); and, in a mixed economy, some resources are owned by both sectors, private and public. Resources are allocated according to the forces of supply and demand.
Government interference in the market mechanism can lead to economic inefficiency when it is applied to some private goods. Prices convey a lot of information. They not only tell producers what to produce but also inform the producers to produce what people want. The more inaccurate the information gets, the lesser will be the economic coordination which will in turn lower satisfaction of wants. Thus interference in the information conveyed by prices is destructive to economic development if misapplied or overused. However, the market mechanism often cannot optimize for public goods, owing to problems such as the tragedy of the commons. For example, modern highways have been good for economic development, but it has taken government planning and allocation to bring them into existence.
Other market mechanisms include government fiscal policy and monetary policy, described by the Friedman rule proposed by Milton Friedman. These policies will influence demand by price adjustments through taxes and charges and through adjustments to the value of money by the related supply of money.

Mark Howard Thiemens is an American geophysicist and chemist whose work spans several areas of the Earth and chemical sciences. He is a Distinguished Professor at the University of California, San Diego, where he continues to be associated with research in these fields.

Thiemens is best known for his role in a significant scientific finding. In 1983, he co-discovered mass-independent fractionation. This discovery is a central part of his professional record and remains one of the most notable achievements connected to his name. The concept relates to how isotopes are distributed in chemical processes, and its identification opened a distinctive line of inquiry within chemistry and geophysics.

His research also includes the atmospheric chemistry of climate change. This focus places his work within the broader effort to understand the chemical processes that take place in the atmosphere and how they relate to a changing climate.

Over the course of his career, Thiemens has received several major honors. In 2008, he was elected to the National Academy of Sciences, a recognition reserved for scientists who have made distinguished contributions to research. In 2017, he was awarded the Leonard Medal. More recently, in 2024, he was elected to the Royal Society, adding another prominent distinction to his record.

Taken together, these milestones reflect a career marked by a foundational discovery, ongoing investigation of atmospheric chemistry, and recognition from respected scientific institutions. As an American geophysicist and chemist based at the University of California, San Diego, Mark H. It was based on Decree-Law No. 2883 of February 27, 1986, which provided the legal foundation for the measures that followed. At the time, José Sarney was president, and Dilson Funaro was Minister of Finance. The main goal of the plan was price control. Price control was the central tool through which the government tried to bring inflation under command.

In its early months, the results appeared striking. The plan reduced inflation from 12.49% in February 1986 to 1.40% in October of the same year. This sharp fall was the most visible achievement of the program, and it showed how large the immediate effect of the new measures could be on the monthly rate of price increases.

However, the approach also produced serious difficulties. Due to price controls, supplies became scarcer. When prices are held down by official measures, the availability of goods can suffer, and this is what happened under the Cruzado Plan. The shortage of supplies became one of the most notable side effects of the strategy and weighed on its overall record.

The plan's reputation was shaped by this contrast between a dramatic decline in inflation and the scarcity that accompanied price controls. Years later, a leading participant offered a clear judgment of the experience. In 2005, José Sarney admitted that the Cruzado Plan was a mistake. His statement stands as a notable assessment of the program, coming from the same person who had served as president when it was launched in 1986.

The channel launched on 1 November 1997 as UK Style. It kept that name for more than a decade. On 30 April 2009, it was rebranded Home, a name that reflected the focus of its programming on interior home and garden subjects.

A further change followed on 21 January 2020, when the channel was rebranded to HGTV. Under that name, it continued to serve viewers in both the United Kingdom and Ireland as a free-to-air service, and it remained under the ownership of Warner Bros. Discovery.

HGTV closed on 13 January 2026. Across its existence, the channel carried three names: UK Style, Home and HGTV. Each name marked a distinct stage in its history, and together they describe the course of a lifestyle channel that was available to audiences across both countries without a subscription.

Air Canada Flight 797 was an international passenger flight from Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport to Montréal–Dorval International Airport with a stop in Toronto. The flight is remembered because of the emergency that unfolded aboard the aircraft on 2 June 1983, when the McDonnell Douglas DC-9 had an in-flight fire around the rear lavatory.

The fire did not stay in one place. It spread between the outer skin and inner decor panels of the aircraft, and as it moved it filled the plane with toxic smoke. Because the flames were hidden in the space behind the interior panels, the situation inside the aircraft became increasingly dangerous for everyone on board.

The fire also burned through crucial electrical cables. This disabled cockpit instrumentation and forced a diversion to Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport. The crew therefore had to deal with both the spreading smoke in the cabin and the loss of important instruments in the cockpit while heading toward an alternative airport.

The accident had a lasting human cost. Canadian folk singer Stan Rogers, age 33, was killed in the accident. His death made the event especially notable in Canada, and his loss is still remembered alongside the history of the flight.

The accident also led to changes in aviation safety rules. New requirements were introduced to install smoke detectors in lavatories and add strip lights marking exit paths. These measures addressed two of the problems highlighted by the fire: the danger of a blaze starting in a hidden area of the aircraft, and the need for passengers to find their way out when smoke fills the cabin. Air Canada Flight 797 is therefore remembered both for the lives lost and for the improvements in safety that followed.

A USB image is a bootable image of an Operating system or other software. Instead of relying on conventional CD or DVD discs, the boot loader is located on a USB flash drive or another USB device. This means the system can be started directly from the USB device.

When it is used, the operating system loads from the USB device like a Live CD. A USB image runs off of the USB device the whole time, so the device stays in use for as long as the system is running.

One practical advantage is portability. A USB image is easier to carry than a conventional CD or DVD, which makes it convenient for people who want to bring an operating system or other software with them and start it wherever a suitable computer is available.

There is one limitation to keep in mind. Some older devices may not support USB booting, so a USB image may not work on every machine.

Tools exist to help create these drives. Ubuntu has included a utility for installing an operating system image file to a USB flash drive since version 9.10.

Living medicine is a way of describing a field that is also called microbial therapy, or microbial therapeutics. The idea is simple to state: instead of relying only on substances that are chemically made, this approach uses beneficial microorganisms as treatments. Because these treatments are alive, microbial therapeutics are sometimes referred to as living medicines.

The microorganisms involved can come from several groups. Beneficial microorganisms can include bacteria, viruses, bacteriophages, and fungi. This range shows that the category is broad and does not depend on a single kind of organism. A treatment may be built around one type of microbe, and the choice depends on what the therapy is meant to do.

Microbial therapeutics may consist of naturally occurring microorganisms or genetically engineered ones. In other words, some living medicines use microbes as they are found, while others use microbes that have been changed through genetic engineering. Both routes fall under the same general heading, since the defining feature is that the medicine itself is a living organism or a group of living organisms.

Several examples help make the concept concrete. Examples of microbial therapeutics include probiotics, live biotherapeutic products, and phage therapy. Each of these belongs to the wider family of living medicines, even though they differ in form and purpose.

Phage therapy offers a clear illustration of how a living medicine can work. It uses bacteriophages to target harmful bacteria. In this case, one kind of microorganism is put to use against another, which shows how the living nature of these treatments sets them apart from other kinds of medicine.

Carswell Grove Baptist Church and Cemetery is located in Jenkins County, Georgia. It is a historic site that combines a place of worship with a burial ground, and it has been recognized for its significance. The property was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1996, a designation that reflects its importance as a historic place.

The history of the site begins in the years after the Civil War. The cemetery was founded around 1870. According to the history of the site, White judge Porter W. Carswell gave blacks 2 acres nearby. That gift is part of the story of how the community around the church and cemetery took shape, and the name of the church and cemetery recalls the judge who made it.

The church itself has faced serious losses over the years. The original church burned in 1919, an event that marked a significant moment in the life of the congregation and the history of the property. The church that stood on the site later was also lost. It was destroyed by arson in 2014, long after it had been placed on the National Register of Historic Places. The destruction of the building in 2014 was a profound loss for the congregation and for those who value the historic character of the property.

Even so, the congregation has continued. Today the congregation meets in a more modest and modern adjacent building built in 2008. This building stands next to the site of the destroyed church and allows regular worship to carry on at the same location where members have gathered for generations. The cemetery, founded around 1870, remains part of the property and continues to connect the present congregation with the people who came before them.

Taken together, these details show a place shaped by gift, loss, and perseverance. From the 2 acres given nearby, to the fire of 1919, to the arson of 2014, and to the building completed in 2008, Carswell Grove Baptist Church and Cemetery in Jenkins County, Georgia, preserves a long and meaningful history that is still carried forward by its congregation.

Carswell Grove Baptist Church and Cemetery (1842–1846 Big Buckhead Church Road, near the hamlet of Perkins, about 7 miles north of the city of Millen, in Jenkins County, Georgia) is a historic Black church and cemetery which are listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1996. The church, a replacement for an earlier church burned in 1919, was destroyed by arson in 2014.
A different historic church, the Big Buckhead Baptist Church, is located a few hundred yards southwest. Prior to the Civil War blacks had worshipped there in segregated pews; "the negroes, whether free or slave, were quiet spectators" because they were considered members of the church with the same status as converted heathens in foreign lands. Yet all received the same communion, and all were baptized in the same water without distinction. After the war and the emancipation of the slaves, there was an impetus by both white and colored congregants to develop separate congregations. White judge Porter W. Carswell gave blacks 2 acres (0.81 ha) nearby to build their own church; they named it in his honor. Over the next five decades, the church became the spiritual heart of the local black community.
The original church was the first of seven black churches burned in the Jenkins County, Georgia, riot of 1919. It was replaced in 1919 by a wood-frame clapboarded building with Gothic Revival windows and other details. Its front gable end was flanked by two square towers. Before its destruction in 2014, the building was boarded up and had deteriorated; the congregation meets in a more modest and modern adjacent building built in 2008.

Born Rashel Lobenstein in New York City, she performed under the stage name Maud Raymond. She began her career in variety theatre in the late 1880s; and established herself as a star in vaudeville and burlesque entertainments beginning in the 1890s as a soubrette. In her early career she was known for her comedic work in the soubrette style and for her performances of ballads and excerpts from operas.
In 1895 she married the comedian Gus Rogers of the Rogers Brothers, and was active in the Rogers Brothers shows in which she excelled in comic portrayals of Dutch and German characters. Some of these shows were performed on Broadway in addition to touring the United States. Raymond also appeared in several Broadway plays and musicals without the Rogers Brothers from 1901 through 1912. Beginning with the part of Topsy in the 1901 Broadway production of Uncle Tom's Cabin some of her parts were performed in blackface. As a vocalist in the first decade of the 20th century she became associated with coon songs and ragtime pieces during her Broadway career. She made several recordings for the Victor Talking Machine Company in 1909-1910 which are catalogued in the Discography of American Historical Recordings.

A cloudbook is a class of laptop computer. The term describes a kind of portable machine that has taken different forms over time, and its history is closely tied to a handful of products and platforms that shaped how people understand it today.

The concept of a cloudbook emerged in 2007 with the cancelled Palm Foleo. Although that device never reached the market, it is remembered as the starting point for the idea. A few years later, in 2010, Google announced a reference design for a cloudbook running ChromeOS. This design laid out how such a laptop might be built and what software it would use.

The first Chromebook models were released in 2011, turning the reference design into products that people could buy. Chromebook found widespread adoption, especially in educational markets, and it became the best-known example of the cloudbook idea.

Competition followed. Microsoft pushed a competing cloudbook platform to Chromebook in the mid-2010s, offering an alternative to the ChromeOS approach. The first such cloudbook released was Acer's Aspire One Cloudbook in 2015.

Taken together, these events outline the story of the cloudbook: an idea that appeared in 2007, a reference design announced in 2010, the arrival of Chromebook models in 2011, and a rival platform that reached the market in 2015.

The Reichskommissariat Ostland was an administrative entity of the Reich Ministry for the Occupied Eastern Territories from 1941 to 1945. It served as the German civilian occupation regime in Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and the western part of the Byelorussian SSR. The name Ostland was applied to this large area of territory under German control, which was governed as a single unit rather than as separate national states.

The Reichskommissariat was established after the success of the Wehrmacht's Baltic operation and an initial period of military administration by Army Group North Rear Area. Once the front had moved eastward and the first phase of the occupation had passed, authority in the region was transferred from the military to a civilian administration answering to the Reich Ministry for the Occupied Eastern Territories.

For administrative purposes, Ostland was divided into four parts: Generalbezirk Estland, Generalbezirk Lettland, Generalbezirk Litauen, and Generalbezirk Weißruthenien. Each of these Generalbezirke corresponded broadly to one of the territories placed under the occupation regime, with Weißruthenien covering the western part of the Byelorussian SSR.

The senior official of the Reichskommissariat held the title of Reichskommissar. Hinrich Lohse served as the Reichskommissar from 1941 to 1944, and Erich Koch held the post from 1944 to 1945. Lohse therefore headed the civilian administration for most of its existence, while Koch took over during its final phase.

The occupation brought mass killing on a very large scale. The SS and their Einsatzgruppen A and B killed over a million Jews and others in the territory. This violence is among the most significant aspects of the history of the Reichskommissariat and of the German occupation in the Baltic region and western Byelorussia.

The German hold on the region did not last. The Red Army recaptured most of Ostland in 1943 and 1944, ending the civilian occupation regime across most of its area. The Reichskommissariat is formally dated to 1945, the final year of its nominal existence, even though most of the territory it claimed had by then been lost.

Keep the Widow Waking is a lost Jacobean play. Although the text has not survived, it remains of interest to students of the period, because its chief significance is the light it throws on collaborative authorship in English Renaissance drama.

The play was licensed by the Master of the Revels in September 1624. The Revels accounts state that John Ford and John Webster wrote it. On this evidence alone, the work would appear to be a partnership between two dramatists. However, another source complicates that picture. Thomas Dekker testified that Keep the Widow Waking was written by Dekker, Ford, Webster, and William Rowley. The two accounts differ in the number of writers they name, and the difference shows how a single play could be credited in more than one way depending on who was describing it.

This pattern is not unique to this one lost play. The Spanish Gypsy was perhaps written by Dekker, Ford, and William Rowley. The uncertainty in that attribution reminds readers that the authorship of plays from this era is often a matter of careful judgment rather than settled fact.

A further example comes from The Witch of Edmonton. The first published text of that play was dated 1658 and stated Dekker, Ford, and Rowley wrote it. Taken together, these cases suggest that shared writing was a familiar way of producing plays, and that the names attached to a work could come from official records, from the testimony of a participant, or from a printed title page issued long afterward.

For readers interested in how plays were made, Keep the Widow Waking therefore serves as a useful case study. Even without its script, the surviving references let us see how several writers might join together on one piece, and how differently their contributions could later be recorded.

An anti-twister mechanism is an arrangement that lets a link run to a rotating object without the link becoming twisted. The link could be an electrical cable or a flexible conduit. Because the connection is carried by a flexible element rather than by sliding contacts, the object can turn while the link stays connected to it.

The mechanism was intended as an alternative to slip rings for supplying electric power to a rotating device. Slip rings use fine metal brushes that slide in contact to provide an electrical path. This sliding contact works, but it has drawbacks. In small devices, the noise from brushing was unacceptable in tiny electronic components. An anti-twister mechanism offers a way around that problem, since the electrical path is a continuous cable instead of a set of brushes rubbing against rings.

One early example is a device patented in 1971 by Dale A. Adams. It used a rotating disk and a cable at half the disk rate. That half-rate relationship is the central idea behind this kind of design: the cable is made to move at a different rate from the rotating object, so that the turning is shared out and the cable does not accumulate twist as the object continues to rotate.

The underlying mathematics connects to a well-known demonstration. Dirac's Plate trick relates to the Spin(3) group represented by unit quaternions called versors. In that demonstration, a plate or similar object can be rotated while it remains attached by flexible connections, and the connections can be kept from tangling through the right pattern of motion. The same kind of reasoning explains why a flexible link can follow a rotating body without being wound up, provided its motion is arranged correctly relative to the rotation.

Taken together, these ideas describe a practical approach to connecting a stationary supply to a rotating device. Rather than relying on brushes sliding over contacts, the mechanism uses a cable or conduit whose movement is coordinated with the rotation, which avoids the brushing noise that troubled small electronic devices.

The anti-twister or antitwister mechanism is a method of connecting a flexible link between two objects, one of which is rotating with respect to the other, in a way that prevents the link from becoming twisted. The link could be an electrical cable or a flexible conduit.
This mechanism is intended as an alternative to the usual method of supplying electric power to a rotating device, through the use of slip rings. The slip rings are attached to one part of the machine, and a set of fine metal brushes are attached to the other part. The brushes are kept in sliding contact with the slip rings, providing an electrical path between the two parts while allowing the parts to rotate about each other.
However, this presents problems with smaller devices. Whereas with large devices minor fluctuations in the power provided through the brush mechanism are inconsequential, in the case of tiny electronic components, the brushing introduces unacceptable levels of noise in the stream of power supplied. Therefore, a smoother means of power delivery is needed.
A device designed and patented in 1971 by Dale A. Adams and reported in The Amateur Scientist in December 1975, solves this problem with a rotating disk above a base from which a cable extends up, over, and onto the top of the disk. As the disk rotates the plane of this cable is rotated at exactly half the rate of the disk so the cable experiences no net twisting.
What makes the device possible is the peculiar connectivity of the space of 3D rotations, as discovered by P. A. M. Dirac and illustrated in his Plate trick (also known as the string trick or belt trick). Its covering Spin(3) group can be represented by unit quaternions, also known as versors.

This relationship between the rotating disk and the cable is the defining detail of the arrangement described in Adams’s 1971 patent.

The anti-twister mechanism is also connected conceptually with Dirac's Plate trick. Dirac's Plate trick relates to the Spin(3) group. The connection therefore proceeds from the plate trick to Spin(3), and from Spin(3) to its representation by unit quaternions, or versors.

Its practical purpose was to replace slip rings in supplying power to a rotating device, especially where brushing noise was unacceptable in the tiny electronic components of small devices. Its described implementation by Dale A. Adams used a cable moving at half the rotating disk’s rate, while its conceptual setting includes Dirac's Plate trick, Spin(3), and versors.
